question: What is the best way to describe a clinical adverse event?

options.A: A natural progression of an underlying disease
options.B: Any normal side effect of a prescribed medication
options.C: A patient refusing to follow hospital treatment rules
options.D: An unintended injury caused by healthcare management

explanation: You've got this! An adverse event simply means accidental harm that happens because of medical care, rather than the illness itself. It helps us know where to improve our care. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why do we want to move away from a 'blame culture' in the hospital?

options.A: It encourages staff to report errors openly so systems can be fixed
options.B: It ensures that hospital management never investigates any mistakes
options.C: It prevents patients from ever filing legal complaints against the hospital
options.D: It allows healthcare workers to ignore basic clinical protocols safely

explanation: Great thinking! When we take away the fear of punishment, everyone feels safe speaking up. That way, our team can catch flaws and fix them together. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h1)

question: What should you do first if a new mother feels very dizzy right after delivery?

options.A: Discharge the patient early to recover in her own home
options.B: Leave the patient alone to finish walking to the bathroom
options.C: Assist the patient safely back to bed and monitor vitals
options.D: Tell the patient to run cold water over her face immediately

explanation: Spot on! Dizziness means she's at risk of a fall. Getting her safely lying down protects her from injury while you check her blood pressure and overall state. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h2)

question: A mother who had spinal/regional anesthesia for her CS wants to walk to the toilet all by herself. What is the safest response?

options.A: Allow her to walk alone since cesarean sections are minor surgeries
options.B: Instruct her to wait until the next morning before moving at all
options.C: Ask a relative to carry her on their back to the restroom
options.D: Stay with her and provide physical support during the walk

explanation: Well done! Regional anesthesia makes legs weak and numb for a bit. Always stay close and support her so she doesn't take a fall. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the single most effective habit to stop germs from spreading around the ward?
explanation: Simple and true! Washing your hands properly is your number one superpower in stopping germs from jumping from person to person. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h3)

question: Why are new mothers and babies extra prone to picking up hospital infections?

options.A: They spend most of their time sleeping in poorly lit hospital rooms
options.B: Their bodies have open wounds and immature or stressed immune systems
options.C: They consume a specialized hospital diet that invites bacteria
options.D: They interact exclusively with medical doctors rather than nurses

explanation: Exactly! Mums have healing places like the uterus or stitches, and babies are still building their immune defenses, making it easier for germs to sneak in. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h3)

question: When is the right time to write down (document) a medication you just gave a patient?

options.A: Immediately after the patient has swallowed or received it
options.B: At the very end of your working shift when sitting down
options.C: Before preparing the drug to save time during the shift
options.D: Whenever the nurse in charge reminds you to do so

explanation: You got it! Documenting right away keeps our records honest and stops accidental double-dosing. Good clinical habit! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h4)

question: Why must strong drugs like oxytocin or magnesium sulfate always be double-checked by a colleague?

options.A: To fulfill a bureaucratic routine that has no actual clinical value
options.B: To delay the medication process so the patient learns patience
options.C: To ensure that the junior midwife takes full blame if a mistake happens
options.D: To catch calculation or preparation errors before the drug harms the patient

explanation: Spot on! High-risk drugs are powerful with tiny safety margins. Two pairs of eyes are always safer than one to protect our mums. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h4)

question: What is the main reason we sort hospital waste into different colored bins?

options.A: To comply with international fashion standards for building design
options.B: To protect staff and handlers from injuries and biological contamination
options.C: To make the hospital waste disposal area look colorful and neat
options.D: To make it easier for patients to throw away their food wrappers

explanation: Brilliant! Color coding keeps needles and infectious waste separate, protecting everyone who handles the rubbish from needle-sticks and infections. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h5)

question: During a night shift, the power goes off and the generator fails while you are suturing an episiotomy. What do you do first?

options.A: Wait patiently in total darkness until electricity returns on its own
options.B: Continue suturing blindly until you finish the procedure by memory
options.C: Activate emergency torchlights or mobile phone lights to secure the area safely
options.D: Leave the patient bleeding on the examination couch and run outside

explanation: Quick thinking! You need light right away to keep things sterile, see what you're doing, and avoid accidental needle pokes in the dark. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h5)

question: How many patient identifiers should you check before giving any treatment?
explanation: You bet! Using at least two checks (like name and hospital number) ensures the right treatment always goes to the right patient. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h6)

question: In the SBAR handover tool, what does the letter 'B' stand for?
explanation: Easy and helpful! 'B' stands for Background, giving your team the quick clinical story of how the patient got to this point. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h6)

question: How would you describe a 'near-miss' in the clinic?

options.A: A surgical procedure that missed the intended organ completely
options.B: A patient who successfully discharged herself against medical advice
options.C: An error that was caught before reaching the patient or causing harm
options.D: A medication dose that was accidentally doubled and harmed a baby

explanation: Spot on! A near-miss is a close call where a mistake almost happened but was stopped just in time. No harm done, but a great learning moment! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h7)

question: Why is it so helpful to report near-misses along with actual mistakes?

options.A: They reveal hidden system flaws that can be fixed before someone gets hurt
options.B: They show that nurses spend too much time writing paperwork
options.C: They are required by law only for statistical record keeping purposes
options.D: They give the hospital legal proof to punish careless staff members

explanation: You nailed it! Catching near-misses lets us fix small workflow cracks before they turn into real emergencies. Every report helps keep our wards safer. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T7#BMP110_U4_T7_h7)
